newsitem.title: INDIA: India state-run Dena Bank lists below issue price.
newsitem.headline: India state-run Dena Bank lists below issue price.

text.p: Dena Bank, the first in a series of Indian state-run banks to launch new issues, was listed on Monday and traded below its issue price, untouched by the euphoria gripping local stock exchanges, brokers said.
Shares of Dena Bank were trading at 28 rupees at midsession on the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE). Dena raised 1.8 billion rupees in November through an initial public offer at 30 rupees a share.
Analysts said Dena Bank's share price was likely to fall further, despite a sudden, 10 percent jump in Indian share prices on the BSE top 30 index since the start of the year.
"The issue pricing was very aggressive and even at these levels, it continues to look overpriced," said Prabhod Agarwal, banking analyst at securities firm James Capel B&K.

India's lumbering state-run banks had planned to raise some 20 billion rupees in the current financial year ended March 31, 1997. Dena Bank and Bank of Baroda set the ball rolling with new issues of 1.8 billion rupees and 8.5 billion respectively.

"We do not expect Bank of Baroda to go below its issue price. Its allotment pattern doesn't look as vulnerable with the bulk of the issue attracting longer-term investors," said an analyst at a U.S. broking firm. The issue is scheduled to be listed next month.
Many banks -- like Corporation Bank and Canara Bank -- put their plans on hold after Bombay's benchmark stocks index fell sharply last year after hitting a three-year low in December.
Bank of India -- picking courage from the recent spurt in Indian share prices -- said last week its 6.75 billion rupee issue would hit the market on February 21.

"The market has been good in the last fortnight. The rise was not really something that was expected and if the rally sustains for a little longer Bank of India will have made the right move," said a banking analyst at a European brokerage.
As part of financial sector reforms initiated in 1991, India's central bank asked state-run banks to strengthen their capital base and reduce bad and doubtful loans.
The banks are raising funds to increase their capital adequacy to meet international standards.

"Overall, these issues are very positive for the sector. There was a paucity of stocks in the finance sector and one had to buy State Bank of India (SBI), said Girish Kumar, banking analyst at Merrill Lynch & Co in Singapore.
State-run SBI is India's largest commercial bank.
"The banking story goes down well with foreign investors and the widening of choice is very positive for the sector," Kumar said.
